title: Phrasing off the beat and vibrato as tonality
summary: DeVore describes playing ahead of or behind the beat, Armstrong and Oliver, and how vibrato gives the hot tone.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: and it doesn't take, it takes a lot of work. But when you say off the beat, do you mean two and four or do you mean like bumping, holding back a little?

Yeah, that's what I mean, holding back. Phrasing, see. Phrasing off the beat. A whole phrase off the beat. In other words, you could start ahead, you end up behind. Play behind, play ahead. Like Louie, see, he, on this tune once in a while, his little instrument goes, he goes, they start out one, two, one, two, see, he holds back and holds and I mentioned that Louie thing because that little introduction always knocked me out. Yeah, well, Louie perhaps did it more than anybody but Joe Oliver, in some respects was even more subtle than Armstrong, the things that I've heard, more shading and stuff. So much of that was involved in how he phrased. Phrasing, attack, and tonality. That's the three things I keep in my mind whenever I play. No matter what. If I take some strange tunes, maybe some pop tune that might be popular right now that somebody requests and we try and play it. I have to do that sometimes, you know, every New Orleans band runs into that to make it hot so it won't sound like some other square playing, you've got to keep the three things in mind. Keep the... Now when I say tonality, I might expound upon that a little bit more. It's the vibrato. That is what gives a man a hot sound as opposed to a legitimate man straight tone. It's the vibrato. You can't... When I talk to, well, like our clarinet players maybe when it's two months, that's all I tell them to do when he plays. Work on that vibrato. Get it so it practically shakes your horn to pieces. Over-emphasize it at first and after a while you can get it so you can control it. Every man's got to have that. That's what gives you the hot sound. A vibrato, a legitimate vibrato is in all the books, you can find in all the books shaking the horn against your lip. I myself do it with my lip. I don't know, just naturally. Do you shake your jaw? I shake my chops, yeah.

like that, huh? And a clarinet man is the same thing, exactly the same way. Our first clarinet man, Dick Ramberg, he had a lot of trouble with that so I kept after him to shake because I'd seen Raymond do that and I'd seen George too. And you know, it's not vibrato all the time. Kid Thomas plays, well, no, he puts, the vibrato is usually at the end of a phrase. It holds a note and shakes it. Yeah, you hold a note and at the end you shake it, you know. But you can have it going in the middle part too but it's most pronounced at the end. That's how the New Orleans musicians get that cracking sound. I'm thinking of Hormann particularly but the other men too.
